I Ditched VS Code For The Open-Source VSCodium, And I Have No Regrets

On I Ditched VS Code For The Open-Source VSCodium, And I Have No Regrets

VS Code is one of the most popular open-source (mostly) applications out there, and for good reason: It does everything you could ask for and then some. However, it also has always-on telemetry that you cannot disable. That is where VSCodium comes into play.
Visual Studio Code is the jack of all trades
Visual Studio Code is one of the most popular apps among programmers,
VS Code’s single biggest advantage is the sheer number of files it can handle, and handle well.

Unlike Word processors (like Microsoft Word, Google Sheets, or the now-defunct WordPad), VS Code won’t accidentally change the formatting of a text file that you open or erroneously insert formatting characters that can break something when you save it. That makes it an extremely popular tool for any kind of work that involves quickly and neatly editing  plain text files .

Additionally, the folder hierarchy view that it supports—where you can add an entire folder rather than just open one file at a time—makes it great if you want to explore all of the editable text files for a program or game. On more than one occasion, I’ve been able to use VS Code to find configuration options that didn’t have any documentation on the internet, and I was having difficulty locating them manually.
The Folder hierarchy view in VSCodium.
If you’re ever going to tweak any kind of text files, it is an invaluable tool to have a round.
VS Code is as good an IDE
While VS Code is technically an advanced text editor, its flexibility and extensibility have elevated it almost to the level of  an integrated development environment.

It features syntax highlighting for hundreds of programming languages as well as “smart” features like IntelliSense, which is a type of language-specific autocomplete for programming languages. It can spot errors, suggest which function you might want as you start typing, or insert pre-written code snippets.

IntelliSense supports JavaScript, Typescript, JSON, HTML, CSS, SCSS, and Less by default, though there are a huge number of extensions available that make it work with most other popular programming languages. Lately, I’ve been using rust-analyzer while learning the Rust programming language.
You just need to install the appropriate extension, and you’re off to the races.
An integrated developer environment and the VS Code logo in the center.
Try these extensions and you’ll wonder how you ever lived without them!
Why replace VS Code with VSCodium?
If Visual Studio Code is so great—and it is—why replace it with VSCodium?

VS Code has one downside: You’re stuck with Microsoft’s telemetry. Despite the fact that most of VS Code is open source, you can’t disable it. If you’re all-in on the free and open-source movement—which is usually very privacy centric—that may be a sticking point for you.
That is where VSCodium comes in.
VSCodium: Everything great about VS Code without Microsoft

VSCodium  is the  fully  open-source variant of VS Code. It is built on exactly the same underlying code as VS Code and is virtually identical in every way. The only major difference is that VSCodium has the compulsory Microsoft telemetry stripped out.
Disabling the telemetry itself won’t impact your experience too much.
However, there are a few proprietary Microsoft extensions available for VS Code that you can’t normally use with VSCodium, though there are some workarounds that exist.
Switching from VS Code to VSCodium
VSCodium is available for all of the major desktop operating systems. If you’re using macOS, you’ll need to use brew to install it.
By subscribing, you agree to receive newsletter and marketing emails, and accept Valnet’s  Terms of Use  and  Privacy Policy . You can unsubscribe anytime.
If you’re on Windows, you can install it using Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, or by running the executable directly.
Windows PowerShell with 'winget' written in the center.
You should check out this overlooked Windows package manager.

I prefer the executable, which is  available on VSCodium’ GitHub Releases page . Once you have it downloaded, I’d recommend tweaking one default installation setting. When prompted, enable the “Add ‘Open with VSCodium’ action to Windows Explorer file context menu.”
Enable the Add VSCodium to the right-click context menu.
I constantly use VSCodium to edit text files. Having it accessible instantly when I right-click is extremely convenient.

The only slight downside here is if you already enabled that option with VS Code, too. It can contribute to  clutter in the right-click context menu , which tends to get a bit messy anyway. As a result, I’d recommend removing VS Code if you’re going to switch over to VSCodium, though there is no real downside to keeping both.
I switched out VS Code for VSCodium a long time ago now, and I use it on every device that supports it. Despite missing a few extensions, I don’t regret it at all, since VSCodium is just as good.
